Question: Can you define, deploy, and manage a heterogeneous team of specialised agents with distinct roles, capabilities, and model assignments working toward a shared goal?
Response: Yes. Our architecture achieves heterogeneous specialisation through skills rather than separate agent processes. A domain-scoped Hosted Agent (e.g. Hiring Agent) runs ephemeral GHCP SDK sessions that load different skills depending on the workflow phase. Each skill has its own distinct role (screening, sourcing, compliance, offer generation), its own declared capabilities and allowed tools, and its own model assignment (a screening skill may use a cheap model for keyword filtering while a candidate evaluation skill uses a frontier model). The outcome is the same as separate agents — specialised capabilities with distinct roles and model assignments working toward a shared goal — but with meaningful architectural advantages: no inter-agent communication overhead, shared workflow context without message passing, simpler governance (one Entra identity per domain rather than per specialist), and easier operationalisation at fleet scale. The Hiring Agent container runs 10+ distinct skills across the hiring lifecycle. The Finance Agent container runs skills across the procure-to-pay lifecycle. Azure Durable Functions coordinates the phase sequencing toward the shared goal. The Fleet Manager governs the fleet.
Key Technologies: GHCP SDK skills (specialisation), Foundry model catalog (tiered models), Durable Functions (coordination), Hosted Agent containers (domain-scoped)
POC Demo: POC2: Show 10+ distinct skills loaded across hiring workflow phases — each with different model assignments and tool access — coordinated by Durable Functions.

Question: What orchestration topologies are supported: sequential, parallel, hierarchical, peer-to-peer, hybrid? Can the orchestrator select pattern dynamically based on task structure?
Response: All topologies are supported through Durable Functions orchestration. Sequential: phase B waits for phase A completion (interview after screening). Parallel: fan-out/fan-in for concurrent execution (sourcing + job design run in parallel). Hierarchical: Fleet Manager oversees domain agents which execute phase-level skills. Hybrid: dynamic combination based on workflow state — Durable Functions evaluates conditions at each phase boundary and selects the next pattern. Dynamic selection: the agentic loop at each phase can reason about dependencies and recommend the next topology. The Durable Functions orchestration implements conditional branching based on phase outputs — if budget approval is pending, sourcing can start in parallel; if compliance flags arise, sequential review is required before proceeding. This is not a static DAG — the orchestration adapts based on runtime data.
Key Technologies: Azure Durable Functions (fan-out/fan-in, conditional, timer), GHCP SDK agentic loops (dynamic reasoning)
POC Demo: POC2: Demonstrate parallel sourcing + job design, sequential offer-after-interview, and dynamic re-routing when compliance flag triggers additional review.

Question: Can agents spawn new sub-agents at runtime? Distinguish persistent (registry-stored, governance-reviewed) vs ephemeral (garbage-collected post-task).
Response: Our architecture natively distinguishes persistent and ephemeral execution. Persistent: skills registered in Azure API Center with lifecycle governance (Design -> Preview -> Production). These are the governed, reviewed capabilities that agents load. A new skill can be authored and registered through the API Center lifecycle — this is the 'persistent agent' equivalent. Ephemeral: every GHCP SDK agentic loop session is ephemeral by design — it spins up for a phase, loads skills and tools, does the work, writes state, emits telemetry, and exits. No long-running processes. The Durable Functions orchestration can dynamically spawn new agentic loop sessions at runtime based on workflow needs (e.g. if 50 CVs need screening, fan out to parallel ephemeral sessions). All ephemeral sessions are garbage-collected after completion — state persists in the durable store, not in the session.
Key Technologies: GHCP SDK ephemeral sessions, Azure API Center (persistent skill registry), Durable Functions fan-out
POC Demo: POC2: Show parallel CV screening — Durable Functions fans out to multiple ephemeral agentic loops, each loading the screening skill, processing a batch, writing results, and exiting.

Question: As workflows stabilise, can orchestration transition from generative (LLM-driven) to deterministic (codified DAGs)? Describe the crystallisation mechanism and version control.
Response: Yes — crystallisation is a core architectural principle. Skills are the crystallisation artefact. Pattern: (1) Observation — the agentic loop reasons through a task using LLM-driven logic (e.g. CV parsing). (2) Validation — after repeated successful execution, the pattern is statistically validated. (3) Code generation — the proven logic is extracted into deterministic code. (4) Review — human reviews the deterministic implementation. (5) Promotion — the crystallised skill is registered in Azure API Center, promoted through Design -> Preview -> Production lifecycle. (6) Monitoring — the crystallised skill runs deterministically (faster, cheaper, more predictable). If it encounters a novel exception it cannot handle, it falls back to generative orchestration and logs the exception for the next crystallisation cycle. Version control: skills are Git-committed SKILL.md files synced to API Center. Each version is immutable once promoted. The crystallisation pipeline is managed through standard CI/CD with approval gates.
Key Technologies: Skill crystallisation pipeline, Azure API Center lifecycle, Git version control, CI/CD approval gates
POC Demo: POC2: Show a CV parsing skill crystallised from generative to deterministic — demonstrate the promotion workflow in API Center and fallback to generative on novel input.

Question: Describe plan-and-execute cost optimisation: tiered model usage (planner vs executor), token budgets, caching, batching, structured outputs.
Response: Cost optimisation is architectural. (1) Tiered model usage: skills specify the appropriate model tier. Keyword filtering and triage use a cheap fast model. Top-30 candidate evaluation uses a frontier model. Budget checks use structured output with a small model. The skill author selects the model; APIM enforces it. (2) Token budgets: APIM AI Gateway enforces per-agent, per-model token rate limits. Skills can declare token budget expectations. (3) Caching: APIM provides semantic caching for repeated similar queries — identical invoice validation queries hit cache instead of model. (4) Batching: Durable Functions fan-out enables batch processing — 50 invoices processed in parallel ephemeral sessions rather than sequentially. (5) Structured outputs: GHCP SDK supports schema-validated responses — the model outputs structured JSON matching a defined schema, reducing token waste and post-processing. (6) Crystallisation: deterministic skills bypass the LLM entirely — proven patterns execute as code at near-zero inference cost. Cost visibility: OTEL telemetry + APIM metrics provide per-workflow, per-phase cost attribution visible on the Control Plane.
Key Technologies: APIM semantic caching and token limits, tiered Foundry models, GHCP SDK structured outputs, skill crystallisation
POC Demo: POC1: Show cost dashboard with per-invoice cost breakdown — tiered model usage visible. Show semantic cache hit rate for repeated validation queries.
